# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Clinical Review of Evidence, Advancements, and Future Directions

## Introduction
For decades, the transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has served as the cornerstone of sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention. However, intravascular leads are vulnerable to biomechanical stress, fractures, venous occlusion, and systemic endovascular infections, which carry high morbidity and mortality. To circumvent these lead-related limitations, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed, offering an entirely extra-thoracic alternative [1]. Early clinical studies and pooled registry analyses confirmed the system's ability to sense, detect, and terminate life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias without entering the heart or vasculature [2,3].

## Clinical Evidence and Safety
The clinical efficacy and safety of the S-ICD have been validated across several large registries and clinical trials. The prospective EFFORTLESS S-ICD registry demonstrated excellent shock efficacy and low complication rates at midterm and long-term (5-year) follow-up [4-6]. These findings were corroborated by the S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS), which documented high real-world efficacy in a diverse patient population [7,8].

Importantly, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have solidified the S-ICD's clinical standing. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial—the first head-to-head RCT comparing the S-ICD to the TV-ICD—demonstrated that the S-ICD is non-inferior to the TV-ICD with respect to the composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [9]. Concurrently, the UNTOUCHED trial proved that utilizing contemporary S-ICD programming and a high-rate cutoff leads to remarkably low inappropriate shock rates in primary prevention cohorts with low ejection fraction, rivaling those of modern TV-ICD trials [10]. To further examine acute safety, the ATLAS trial showed a 92% reduction in serious lead-related complications at six months post-implantation with the S-ICD compared to transvenous systems [11]. Long-term observational cohorts and propensity-matched studies comparing S-ICD and TV-ICD recipients have highlighted stable, sustained defibrillation efficacy alongside significantly fewer lead-related interventions over time [12-14]. Consequently, current guidelines from both the AHA/ACC/HRS and the ESC recommend the S-ICD as a Class IIa (and in some instances Class I) indication for patients who have an ICD indication but no requirement for bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) [15,16].

## Anatomical Screening, Implantation, and Procedural Refinements
Successful S-ICD therapy relies heavily on appropriate patient selection and precise device positioning. Electrocardiographic (ECG) screening is mandatory to avoid T-wave oversensing, which can be performed using manual template screening or automated software tools [17,18]. Surgical implantation has also evolved. While the original method utilized a three-incision technique, a two-incision technique omitting the superior parasternal incision has become the standard of care due to improved cosmetic outcomes and reduced procedural times without compromising sensing or defibrillation efficacy [19].

To evaluate implant quality, the PRAETORIAN score was developed to estimate the risk of defibrillation failure based on chest radiographs [20]. Historically, a routine intraoperative defibrillation threshold (DFT) test was performed to verify conversion efficacy. However, the landmark PRAETORIAN-DFT trial successfully showed that PRAETORIAN score-guided omission of DFT testing is non-inferior to routine DFT testing for first-shock conversion of spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias, thereby reducing procedural risk and the need for deep sedation [21].

## Inappropriate Shocks, Device Longevity, and Tricuspid Valve Preservation
Inappropriate shocks, primarily caused by T-wave oversensing or supraventricular tachycardias, remain a clinical challenge [22,23]. To mitigate this risk, advancements such as the "SMART Pass" high-pass filter have been integrated into S-ICD sensing algorithms, yielding a substantial reduction in inappropriate therapies [24,25]. Furthermore, contemporary registries indicate that systemic infections are rare and usually confined to the subcutaneous pocket, avoiding the catastrophic endocarditis risk seen with TV-ICDs [26].

Additionally, concerns regarding S-ICD battery longevity have been resolved. Although earlier generations had high current drain, modern S-ICD systems have demonstrated an estimated real-world battery longevity of approximately 6 to 9 years [27,28]. Furthermore, S-ICDs preserve right ventricular and tricuspid valve function. Intracardiac leads often cause mechanical trauma, leading to worsening tricuspid regurgitation (TR) [29]. S-ICD patients are significantly less likely to develop TR compared to those with TV-ICD leads [29].

## Future Frontiers
The primary limitation of S-ICD therapy has been its inability to deliver bradycardia pacing or ATP. To address this, modular cardiac rhythm management systems have been introduced. The MODULAR ATP trial validated a system in which a leadless pacemaker implanted in the right ventricle communicates wirelessly with an S-ICD to deliver ATP when ventricular tachycardia is detected, combining the benefits of intravascular lead avoidance with therapeutic pacing [30].

## Conclusion
The S-ICD represents a paradigm shift in device-based sudden cardiac death prevention. Supported by robust randomized trials, S-ICD therapy offers comparable defibrillation efficacy to TV-ICDs while significantly reducing lead-related complications and preserving valvular function. With refinements in sensing algorithms, the validation of DFT-free protocols, and the clinical introduction of communicative leadless pacing systems, S-ICD therapy will continue to expand its footprint in electrophysiology.
